To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the brains of Down's syndrome patients who died in their fifties showed more plaques and tanges and a greater relative loss of nerve cell bodies than the brains of younger Down's patients, and that the relative losses in the older Down's patients were smaller than those in patients with Alzheimer's Disease.
the number of plaques, tangles and damaged neurones is greater in the brains of older Down's patients than in the brains of young Down's patients or young normal people.

in Down's syndrome there is an earlier onset, more severe, more diffuse, and less specific pattern of neurofibrillary degeneration and Alzheimer-type pathology, and that the clinical and pathological features are not simply a reflection of the increased life expectancy in this population.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the brain in Down's syndrome and in Alzheimer's disease.
the relationship between brain damage and mental handicap.
the study of the brain in patients with Down syndrome, and in particular with the study of Alzheimer's Disease in these patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Down's syndrome patients show a pattern of brain damage at middle age which is qualitatively identical with that seen in Alzheimer's disease but quantitatively less severe in many regions.
in Down's syndrome, at middle age, the same pathological process operates as in Alzheimer's disease, but that the extent and distribution of the damage is less.

the neuropathology of Down's syndrome is similar to that of Alzheimer's disease in the sense that it is a diffuse degenerative process, but it differs in the sense that the degeneration is less severe and more widespread in Down's syndrome than in Alzheimer's disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

in Down's syndrome, as in Alzheimer's disease, the hippocampal formation is the first area of brain to show the neuropathological changes of Alzheimer's disease, but in the older Down's patients the process is less severe and the changes are less likely to spread to other areas of cortex.
the brains of the younger Down's patients showed no evidence of Alzheimer's disease but that the brains of older Down's patients showed evidence of Alzheimer's pathology.

Down's syndrome patients over 53 have the same neuropathological changes in the brain as patients of similar ages with Alzheimer's disease but with a less severe degree of neuronal loss in the cortex and subcortex.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brains of Down's syndrome individuals are more resistant to the effects of Alzheimer's disease pathology.
the brain of a Down's syndrome patient is more vulnerable to Alzheimer pathology than that of a normal person.
the brains of patients with Down syndrome are different from those of people with other forms of dementia, such as Alzheimer’s, even if they have the same number of plaques.
